title: trace-synth-replayer-residency-cliff-reproducer
body:
Purpose:

Short: define and record a small, repeatable harness that reproduces sharp residency cliffs and eviction cascades observed in production when a small subset of keys spike concurrently with tenant churn. This doc documents the harness (trace-synth replayer), config space explored, telemetry captured, key findings, and actionable mitigations to try in next sprint.

Background / motivation:

- Production symptom: sudden tail-latency spikes (~99.9th token latency) and NVMe read bursts correlated with eviction surge events. Root traces show rapid decay of reuse for a small hot keyset after a burst of high-cardinality short requests.
- Existing KV investigations cover many angles (prefetching, hotset skew, bank-aware pinning), but we lacked a compact, deterministic replay harness that can induce the same cascade starting from a small seed of synthetic traffic plus tenant churn (route migrations, resource pressure).

High-level hypothesis:

- Eviction cascade occurs when: (1) a hot mini-set (H) is being actively referenced and resident; (2) a sudden surge in low-reuse keys (S) from a different tenant or route triggers mass allocations/spillbacks; (3) eviction policy (LRU-ish with aging) demotes H entries because S entries pollute recency windows and cause large, correlated NVMe reads; (4) the NVMe IO increases read-amplification which stalls prefetch threads leading to more misses and a positive feedback loop.

What this harness does:

- Synthesizes request streams parameterized by: hotset size, hotset access rate, background churn rate, multi-tenant interleaving factor, sequence length distribution, per-request KV footprint (num tokens => KV pages touched), and arrival burstiness (pareto/poisson mix).
- Replays deterministic pseudo-random key IDs mapped to page-aligned addresses (so we can test page-boundary fragmentation effects).
- Emits detailed telemetry hooks that map each request to: hit/miss, eviction candidates, before/after residency snapshot, NVMe read size and latencies, memory-bandwidth counters (from perf counters exposed), and per-bank queue depth (when available).

Quick reproducible command (local profiler VM):

1) build replay binary: 
   ./build/replay-synth --mode=local --out=run-20250304.log 

2) run standard repro: 
   ./replay-synth --hotset=512 --hot-rps=1200 --bg-rps=1800 --burst-window-ms=200 --interleave=2 --seqlen-dist=mix-16-256 --duration-s=600 --pin-cores=2-6 --nvme-qos=default 

3) collect telemetry (script included):
   scripts/collect-run-metrics.sh run-20250304.log run-20250304-metrics.tar.gz

Observed signals to collect in each run (must be present in harness output):

- reuse_rate_by_key_percentile: 50, 90, 99 for keys in H and S
- eviction_events_per_second and eviction_batch_sizes histogram
- prefetch_miss_ratio and prefetch_latency_ms P50/P95/P99
- nvme_read_bytes/sec, nvme_ios/sec, nvme_avg_latency_ms
- memory_bandwidth_gb/s (read, write) per NUMA node
- stall_time_due_to_io_ms aggregated by serving thread
- resident_fraction_by_page (heatmap snapshot every 10s)

Small sample snippet of harness output (sanitized):

[2025-03-04T10:12:23Z] RUN START id=run-20250304 hotset=512 bgset=100k
[2025-03-04T10:15:01Z] HOT: key=0x7a1f hits=8 miss=0 reuse=0.88
[2025-03-04T10:15:01Z] BACKGROUND: key=0x9cf2 hits=0 miss=1 reuse=0.01
[2025-03-04T10:16:12Z] EVICT: key=0x7a1f evicted_reason=age score_pre=0.92 score_post=0.14
[2025-03-04T10:16:12Z] NVME: read_issue=12 size=2.1MB lat=14.2ms
[2025-03-04T10:16:12Z] STALL: thread=shard-3 stall_io_ms=32

Experiment matrix we ran (representative subset):

- axis A: hotset size = [64, 256, 512, 2048]
- axis B: hot-rps = [200, 600, 1200, 2400]
- axis C: bg-rps = [500, 1000, 1800, 4000]
- axis D: burst-window-ms = [50, 200, 1000]
- axis E: interleave factor (tenant mixing) = [1 (pure single-tenant), 2, 4]\n- axis F: pinning policy = [none, soft-pin-hot, bank-aware-pin]

Key findings (summary):

1) Sharp residency cliff is most reproducible when hotset size is small (64–512) and hot-rps is high relative to background. Intuition: a concentrated hotset yields high recency score that can be knocked down quickly by pollution.

2) Interleaving factor >=2 (i.e., other tenant traffic interspersed) increases probability of eviction cascade by ~3x versus single-tenant replay. The mixing disrupts recency windows and makes eviction candidates more correlated across shards.

3) Burst-window matters: very short, intense bursts (50–200ms) generate larger eviction batches and NVMe read amplification than prolonged moderate bursts because the runtime tries to satisfy allocation instantly and spills large contiguous spans to NVMe, which then optimize poorly for coalesced reads.

4) Bank-aware pinning reduces read amplification by ~40% in our synthetic runs: mapping hotset pages to separate banks lowered eviction overlap and allowed NVMe reads to be better coalesced across smaller regions.

5) Prefetch strategy sensitivity: aggressive prefix prefetch reduces miss rate for hotset H (improves P99 latency) but increases contention on prefetch worker threads during background surges; if prefetch threads are starved because NVMe IO has saturated, the system still collapses — so prefetch alone is not a silver bullet.

Representative numbers (median over a 10m-run cluster of 3 machines, synthetic config above):

- baseline (no pin): nvme_read_bytes/sec = 230MB/s, nvme_avg_lat = 17.2ms, eviction_events/s = 450, p99 token latency = 540ms
- bank-aware pin: nvme_read_bytes/sec = 140MB/s, nvme_avg_lat = 9.8ms, eviction_events/s = 210, p99 token latency = 220ms

Detailed observations / interesting traces:

- Trace A (hotset=512, hot-rps=1200, bg-rps=1800, burst=200ms): eviction batch sizes showed a bimodal distribution around 8 and 128 pages. The 128-page evictions correlated with short bursts where allocator required new contiguous slots.

- Trace B (hotset=64, interleave=4): eviction wave knocked out >70% of hotset over 900ms, NVMe read tail latencies spiked to 50–80ms for multiple seconds leading to understaffed prefetch workers and cascading misses.

- CPU backpressure: on runs with high background traffic we observed host CPU saturation in the IO worker pool which increased per-eviction processing time and amplified eviction rate. This suggests tuning worker threads / offloading heuristics as an operational lever.

Hypotheses refined (with evidence):

- H1: Cross-tenant interleaving accelerates demotion because recency windows are size-limited and per-shard aging was too aggressive. Evidence: repeatable scaling of eviction rate vs interleave factor.

- H2: Allocation strategy that prefers contiguous region allocation under pressure leads to large eviction batches and NVMe read bursts. Evidence: 128-page eviction modes appear when allocator cannot find small holes.

- H3: Prefetch starvation under NVMe saturation is a key amplifying factor. Evidence: prefetch_latency P99 increased from 6ms to 44ms at the collapse point while prefetch_miss_ratio rose concurrently.

Immediate mitigations to try (quick experiments):

- Reduce aging aggressiveness when per-shard eviction rate > threshold (empirical guardrail) -> small A/B in harness.
- Add soft pinning (preferentially keep top-N hot pages resident for tenants marked as high-qos) and test fairness impact.
- Allocation fragmentation mitigation: prefer small-slot allocation under high churning to avoid 128-page eviction mode.
- Throttle admission of new low-reuse keys under detected NVMe saturation.

Longer-term proposals:

- Implement per-tenant recency windows with adaptive sizing (small hotsets get a proportionally larger window under contention).
- Make prefetch worker pool adaptive to NVMe latency signals (scale workers up when IO latency rises and down when idle).
- Instrument an eviction rollback / fast-reinstate path to reduce tail when accidentally evicting hot entries; measure cost of re-instating vs keeping them pinned.

Open questions / TODOs:

- Q1: Can we reproduce same cascade when using real production request shapes from anonymized traces (next step: craft trace-synth profiles from production sample)?
- Q2: How does multi-node coordination (distributed eviction signals) change behavior vs single-host runs? Need cluster-mode runs.
- Q3: Best metric for automatic detection: eviction_rate vs nvme_read_bytes vs prefetch_latency — which yields earliest reliable signal?

Next immediate actions (owners):

- Aisha: push harness improvements to expose per-bank occupancy histograms and add an opt-in throttle for admission (PR #42). target: 2025-03-10 (WIP).
- Priya: run cluster-mode reproduction on staging with anonymized production trace sample (ticket INF-3124). target: 2025-03-07.
- Diego: prototype soft-pin policy and run A/B against bank-aware pin approach. target: 2025-03-14.

Notes to self / ephemeral ideas:

- It might be useful to test non-uniform page sizes for hotset vs background to simulate model kv varying footprint (e.g., embedding keys vs chat context).
- Consider measuring NVMe scatter-gather patterns — are our reads coalesced or highly random? That maps to controller caching behavior.
- Quick experiment: simulate slow prefetcher by sleeping prefetch worker and see collapse threshold shift.

Attachments and raw artifacts (in repo):

- scripts/ (replay configs, run collectors)
- runs/20250304/ (raw logs, metric tars, heatmap PNGs)
- tools/trace-synth/ (source for harness)

If you want to reproduce fast: clone https://github.com/redwood-inference/replay-synth (WIP PR linked above) and use the replay config under configs/repro/hot-cliff-512.json.

If this looks useful I'll convert the short-term mitigations into concrete experiments in the next sprint and link them to INF backlog items.

-- Aisha
